newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor opposes cutting pollution in 2000.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor opposes cutting pollution in 2000.

text.p: U.S. labour leaders declared their opposition this week to a pending international agreement to curb pollution in industrialised nations, union officials said Friday.
The agreement, expected to be completed in December, would update the 1992 Rio Treaty to stem global warming by requiring industrialised countries to cut their carbon emissions after 2000.
The White House wants to delay implementation until after 2010.

Unions fear that if the United States agrees to new limits on carbon emissions, which largely come from the burning of fossil fuels, industries might trim output from U.S. plants and shift jobs to countries not subject to the same caps.

The executive council of the AFL-CIO passed a resolution Thursday saying nations involved in the negotiations had made a "fundamental error" in exempting rapidly growing countries like China and Brazil from any new pollution restrictions.
"Such an uneven playing field will cause the loss of high-paying U.S. jobs in the mining, manufacturing, transport and other sectors," the resolution said.

The resolution urged the Clinton administration and Congress to reject any agreement that did not include "appropriate commitments from all nations to reduce carbon emissions" and a schedule that avoided "unfair and unnecessary job loss in developed economies."

One industry group said the resolution was passed over the objections of the Democratic administration, but a senior U.S. official said the wording in the final resolution was not far from the administration's view.
"If you look at the bottom lines for this, we don't disagree," said Assistant Secretary of State Eileen Claussen.
"We think the ongoing negotiations should insist upon appropriate commitments (from developing countries). We just don't think they're the same for all countries," she said.
Mineworkers, concerned that carbon emissions limits will stifle coal use, pushed for more universal standards.

"We just haven't seen it for real yet, that there's any serious commitment (by the administration) to do anything besides show leadership regarding countries like China," said Eileen Goldsmith, spokeswoman for the United Mine Workers of America.

The Clinton administration last month proposed industrialised countries should only have to start meeting emissions targets from 2010 onwards, to give industries enough time to develop and adopt new technologies. The plan won muted praise from industry groups, which had been the most vocal critics of the climate change talks.
